speaker: Speaker 1
words: From Kuski, Idaho, and this is the Rural Woman's Oral History Project. Betty, what is your maiden name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was Betty Virginia Tease.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And when were you born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: February 25th, 1938.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where were you born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Spokane, Washington.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where was your first home in Idaho?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I grew up on a farm five miles west of Worley.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you were just born in Idaho, so you never did have to immigrate here or anything?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, my folks lived there. I lived in the same house from the time I was born until I got married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And how old were you when you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was 16. 16.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And how did your family get around when you were a little girl?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, they had an old car. I think it was about a 1930 Chevrolet. And then later, I imagine when I was about five years old, he had an old, old pickup.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now I'm going to ask you a few questions about your family background. And we'll start with your mother's family. What was your mother's maiden name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Bernadine Huizington.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What nationality is that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The last name is English, but she's a mixture of about seven different nationalities. Oh, wow.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was going to ask if there is any particular nationality that had settled the area that your parents lived in.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mostly English and German.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what was your mother's occupation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, she just worked helping the farmer's wives up until she got married, and she's a housewife.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And when was your mother born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In 1906, July 8th.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what was your place of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, she called it the Big Bend Country. It was over around Cooley Dam somewhere.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The Big Bend Country. I wonder why they called it that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it was just a big, dusty desert. It's where all the dust storms blow from up and around.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Like a dust bowl? Uh-huh. Hmm. And your mother's still living?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. When was your mother married?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. And now your father, what was your father's name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: John Henry Teese.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what was his occupation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He's a farmer, and then later he worked as a carpenter, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did he have a wheat farm, or what kind of a farm did he have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mostly wheat, little oats and barley, and then he grew some grass seed, and he raised his own hay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: About how large was his farm?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just 160 acres.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were farms generally smaller then, the wheat farms, than they are now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In that area, but his was one of the smallest ones around.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Wow. And he made it all right on that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, that's all he did until after I was married, and then he started carpentering for my cousin.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Hmm. And when was your father born?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where was he born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Fairfield, Washington.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And your father's also living? Yeah. Living now, too. And did you have any sisters or brothers?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've got one sister, Arlene Glenda Kohler.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Where does Arlene live now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In Coeur d'Alene.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Coeur d'Alene, where... Okay. Now I'll ask you about your immediate family. What is your husband's name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Robert Melvin Smith.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what's his occupation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He's a logger, but the last six years he's worked as an outfitter and guide whenever there's a hunting season open for anything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What is an outfitter?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, they take out-of-state hunters out, and he used to set up hunting camps and have horses, but he's gotten rid of all of them, and he mainly guides now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what about his trapping? Is that still an occupation, or does he do much of that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In the wintertime, he traps.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What does he trap?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Bobcats and coyotes, mainly.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then what does he do with the animals after he traps them?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He sells them to the fur buyer.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What is his date of birth?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where was he born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Aberdeen, Washington.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what was the date and the place where you were married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We were married in Coeur d'Alene, Idaho, in 1954.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And how old is your husband now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Forty-two.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I can hardly remember. And what are your children's names?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've got five children, Terry Lee, Theodore Joe, Kelly Lynn, Becky Sue, and Shelly Terina.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And are any of them working?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The two oldest boys both work in the woods.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do they do?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They're loggers, mainly hooking.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do they work for a logging company?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They worked with their dad. They contracted a job last year, but this year they hope to go to work for one of the other loggers.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That sounds like a pretty good job.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And Teddy is working in a sawmill right now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And Teddy is how old?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He's 18.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And how old is Terry?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And Terry did something interesting just recently, didn't he?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, he was in that movie, Break Heart Pass. He worked as a cavalryman, and he also played an Indian for a couple days.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And how did he get into that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, he just heard that they needed some local people for the cavalry. And he went down there, and they told him to come back on a certain day. And they signed him up.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did he enjoy it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He had a lot of fun. He really liked most of the stars that he got to work with.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He got to know them?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Most of them. They didn't see too much of the star, Charles Bronson, but this Ben Johnson, he really got to know him. In fact, we think someday he might come out and go bear hunting with us.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that's pretty interesting.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: If Terry wants to guide him on a bear hunt.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that would really be fun. Okay, what about your education?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I went just two years to high school, and I quit and got married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what skills have you learned throughout your life?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, just a little bit of everything. When I was still at home, I helped my dad in the fields. He didn't have a boy to help him, so I did it. And I drove tractor in the hay field. And when I was old enough, I learned to drive grain truck and haul wheat. And I milked cows and did gardening. Then later, when I got married, well, I, of course, learned to cook and sew. And I helped build our house. I put the roof on and put the floor in and what I could do. And I like to do minor home repairs. I can wire light fixtures and plug-ins. And I like to overhaul lamps and things like that. I love to bake bread. I do all the painting here in the house. And I like to sew. I made my drapes, and I make a lot of my girls and my own clothes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Reupholster?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I reupholstered a chair. And I've learned to knit and crochet. And most of the time, I'm pretty busy cooking for the hunters.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's a pretty big job. About how many hunters do you cook for all the time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, of course, I've got a large family, so I always include them. But I've cooked for as many as 22 or 23 people.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you've even chopped a little wood in your day and done a few things like that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Until my boys got big enough to do it, I chopped most of my own wood. Wow. I'm here alone so much that I had to learn to do it or I'd freeze.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What are your hobbies or your other interests outside of work around the home?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, that keeps me pretty busy, but in the summer, I do like to go swimming. Of course, I always had to go with the kids when they were small. And we like to go out hiking and take movies.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you swim right out here in the river at all, or do you swim elsewhere?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, no, just the river. The river. The first time I got in a pool, I just about couldn't swim.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: A little bit different. What to you are some of the advantages or the disadvantages of living here in a rural area?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, the shopping isn't as good as closer to a bigger town. If we want to buy a lot of groceries, cases of things, we have to go to Lewiston. And, of course, when you're looking for clothes, you don't get near as big a choice. But as far as I know, that's the only disadvantage there is to living away from a city.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about your medical facilities and all that? Are they pretty adequate?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not really. Anything seriously wrong, we go to Lewiston. The doctors here are okay for a penicillin shot, but if it's serious, I like to go to a specialist.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about the advantages of living here? What would you...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think for kids it's so much better. They're away from all this city life, and they learn to get out and work. And we've got this mountain here above our place, and my boys practically grew up on that mountain. And they've learned to hunt. And I think one boy spent a night out in the woods alone one fall. He got separated when they were out hunting, and he knew where he was, but it got dark, and he couldn't see to get back. And he made it just fine. He knew enough to lay down in one place, and he said he even slept part of the night, and he didn't panic. I was real proud of him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think your boys are pretty self-sufficient? You know, they can take care of themselves if they had to and everything?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think that they could in this kind of a country, but if they went to a city, they would just be lost.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How would you compare your life, the life of a rural woman, with that of an urban woman?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I wouldn't trade with them. I like being out where we can be fairly by ourselves and not a lot of people around. I don't think the crime is as bad. I'm not afraid to let the boys walk to the neighbors after dark. And we never lock our doors at night until we go to bed. We don't have to worry. Of course, we got enough dogs to warn us if anyone comes around. Even for entertainment, I think it's so much cheaper in the city. Anything you want to do to have fun, you have to pay. It costs money. And here, if you want something to do, you can drive for a mile and you're by the river, and you can have a picnic or go swimming or hunt mushrooms and pick flowers. It doesn't cost you anything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you do a lot of that with your kids?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. When the weather's nice, we're always out by the river.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: In the summertime, you do a lot of things outdoors together.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, it's so much cooler. You can drive up the river and when you hit the 23-mile mark, you can just feel the temperature dropping. And on the weekends, we like to go up and stay until evening, and then we come back to town. And you just feel the heat when you drive into town. It's so much hotter here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you don't think you would trade for the life of a city woman? You like it here in the city life?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, definitely.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How does your family life now compare to family life when you were a child?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it's quite different. Out on the farm, it seemed like my dad was always busy. Sunday was no different than any other day. If there was work to be done, he did it. And we hardly ever went anywhere. And there was no one to play with but just my sister. Company was one of the biggest deals there could be. We were thrilled to death when we seen a car coming. And, of course, here we have company nearly all the time. My kids have never been alone. Of course, there's a lot of the hunters that stay with us. I enjoy people. I like to be around people, and I would get lonesome if I lived on a farm where I didn't see anyone.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You think a lot of people today have forgotten how to be alone?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I do. And I think they've forgotten how to get along without the modern things like televisions. When ours broke down, I was glad. It was so peaceful. And we played cards, and of course we had the radio and the phonograph. And we liked to play games together in the evening, checkers or any kind of games. And I really didn't miss the TV at all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's good. I don't like TV much myself. How was your life then financially compared to now? Were you more self-sufficient? Or were you... Did you have much money?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. My folks were really quite poor when I was born. And they just had the small farm, and up until he got the farm paid for, things were really tough. Like when I was in the first grade, I think I had two winter dresses. And my mother made them, and I can remember she even made my coats. And we got two pairs of shoes a year. We got a pair to start school, and then usually about February we would have to have another pair. And those would have to last us until the next fall.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your mother make a lot of the things that you would buy now, like soap and just around the house things, clothes, and things that people just think nothing of buying today?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. She made nearly all of our clothes. She even made our underwear. She made us flannel bloomers, which I hated, but they were sure warm. And I had to wear the old long brown socks because we had so far to walk to school, and it was so cold.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about heating and all that? Did you have a wood stove?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They always had a wood stove, and she always did her own canning, and like you said, making soap.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did she do any spinning or weaving herself?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not that I can remember of. I don't think she did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about free time? What did you used to do with your free time back in the old days?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I remember I used to get awful lonesome, and in the summer especially when it was hot, we had an awful time trying to find a way to entertain ourselves. Because like I said, I only had one sister, and she was nearly four years older than I was. But it seemed as though there was always something to do if we really wanted to do it. But you know, kids, they get bored.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You couldn't just get in the truck, though, and drive off into the country for a few days?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we hardly ever did that. A picnic was really a big deal then.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, it was kind of an extravagance, wasn't it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we had to go so far to find a lake or real woods or anything like that, and it seemed like Dad was always busy. He worked awful hard. What time? Long hours.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What were some of the things that you and your sister did when you were children to occupy yourselves?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we both liked dolls. We played dolls an awful lot together. And we had this little game where we pretended to be teenagers. We even made up a favorite name for each other.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What were your names? Do you remember?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think that mine was Peggy. I can't remember for sure, but we even had a pretend boyfriend. I remember his name was Dwayne, and my sister's was Glenn, until we outgrew that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you expected to go on to school, to high school or anything?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, my sister graduated from high school. She was valedictorian of her class, but I was never real good in school. Oh, I got passing grades, but when I got up around the seventh grade, I didn't really enjoy school. And then I met Bob, and we knew each other for nearly two years. And I think my folks knew in the back of their minds that I was going to get married before I finished.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How old were you when you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I lacked three months of being seventeen. But we came from a real small school. There was only thirty-five in the whole high school. And it wasn't the ideal school. You didn't have much choice of what subjects you took. And I never really thought too much about what I wanted to be. I just knew I was going to get married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did you meet Bob?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's a long story. My sister met his little brother in the bus depot in Spokane. And I was with her, but I never said nothing to him. And he took her name and address, and he was my age. And about a year later, Bob decided he wanted a right to a girl. He was too bashful to go meet one. So he wrote to my sister, and they wrote for maybe six months, when one day he came to see her. And she already had a boyfriend. So she told me not to let her boyfriend know that Bob had come to see her. So I just acted like I knew him. And, oh, he got kind of serious right away, and I told him I was too young to get serious, and it hurt his feelings, and he thought I didn't like him. And so he brought his younger brother up and thought I might like him. It was quite a mix-up before we finally decided that I knew that he was the one I wanted.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But it could get complicated with all those sisters and brothers in there. It did. Very. Well, how old was Bob when you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was almost 21. He just lacked a month.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you had known he and his brother for about two years before you got married? Yes. What do you remember about the things you did together during your courtship, you know, before you married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We didn't get to do very much because he was too poor, and he had to drive about 180 miles to see me. And so when he would come up, he would always stay a few days. And we never did have the money to go anywhere. We just stayed there at home, and I guess we watched TV in the evenings, and we used to go for walks after it cooled off. And then later on, he brought my sister and I both down here to meet his folks, and we spent about four days here. And one night, or one day, his mother and two brothers and his sister took my sister and I all for a ride up in the mountains, and we got stuck in the mud and ended up staying overnight in his old pickup. And I remember that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, Betty, what about your early married life? What were some of your expectations before marriage, and have those been met?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think the only thing I really thought about too much was just making a good home and both of us being happy. And we've had some rough times, but I think we have succeeded. Yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What time did you set it up, North Star Radio? Well, you know, it did say... That noise in the background, that's a two-way radio, isn't it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, my husband and sons got them, and they come in handy when they're bear hunting.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mm-hmm. Get messages back home and everything. Right. Well, that would make me feel a lot more comfortable if I knew that they were all right out there.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Except when they're down in the canyons, I can't reach them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that very often?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, yeah, quite a bit of the time. He has to be up on top of the ridge.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mm-hmm. When you were having your children, what kind of medical services were available to you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, just the ordinary all-around type doctor. Mm-hmm. All of them, but the last one was born in a hospital, and I had the last one at home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You did? Now, who helped you to do that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There's an old doctor that will deliver them once in a while. He said he's getting too old to do that all the time, but I talked him into it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, wow.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And it was great.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You really liked it, huh?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. If I had it to do over again, I'd have all five of them at home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that sounds fascinating. What kind of things affected the number of children you have had? Did you decide how many you wanted to have, or did you just...?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we had the first two boys right away. I wanted the first one. I really wanted a baby. And then I decided that I didn't want to have him grow up alone and so far apart like I was, so we had the second one. And then later on, I got to thinking it would be nice to have another one, and so we had another one, and they were all boys, and I was awful disappointed when I had the third boy. And I said that's all I wanted. And then years later, for medical reasons and because I still wanted a little girl, well, we decided to have another one. And the last one was unplanned.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, she was kind of a surprise.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I guess.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She's a doll, though. What do you see as the future for your children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I expect the boys to grow up pretty much following their dad in the logging and hunting and guiding business, and the girls are too young to tell.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have any ideas of what you'd like them to do, or is it up to them?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's mainly up to them. The two oldest boys don't really have the education to do any business-type work. They weren't very good in school, and they didn't like school. So I imagine they'll pretty much be loggers.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about the girls? Are they really too young for you to tell just yet?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, really. We'll just have to wait until they're older and see.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you think back, what have you done to help support the family?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I do what I can to save money. I can all of the fruit and vegetables that I can get. And I bake my own bread most of the time. And I make most of my cakes from scratch. And once in a while I do sewing jobs that I get paid for. Last fall I bought alkyds and sold them to the fur buyer, which you don't make an awful lot. But then we let a friend stay here during the week, and he paid us for staying. And I saved the money that I got from that and the hides and different little jobs and managed to almost pay for a dishwasher with it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, my gosh. You got your own dishwasher.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Which I have been wanting for quite a while.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, when you feed as many as 22 men at a time, I think you deserve one.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It really helps.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do these things compare with what you did maybe 30 years ago? Have things changed quite a bit for you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, not in the way of cooking, no, because I learned to can and bake bread and all that before I was married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let's see. Have you ever thought of what you would do if something happened to Bob?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I used to think about it. I thought that I would like to be a beautician since I didn't finish high school. That is one job that I could do where I wouldn't need a high school education. And I do like to work with hair.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what about you would rather work then outside of the home than try to do something else?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I would rather, but I just don't know of any way that you could stay home and support a family.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: All those children of yours.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Without help.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever displayed anything in a county fair, any of your work or anything like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I haven't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What suggestions would you give a young woman that would best prepare her for farm life or life in a small town?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, mainly to be able to cook and sew and to manage her money the best that she knows how and to always put her family first, to try to make them happy. I think if a family is happy, you can survive almost any hardship there is.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think that too. I think a lot of, do you feel a lot of young women today don't understand those kind of things? Then you were saying about the young women today.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think a lot of them have been babied too much and a little spoiled. I have seen some of them that had sort of a selfish attitude. They knew what they wanted and they were going to get it. And you have to sacrifice a lot.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you ever feel that you're not satisfied with your life or that you're overworked or anything or taken advantage of?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Sometimes, yes. When I really get tired, I think I have a tendency to think that I'm being used once in a while, but it just lasts until the next day and I get over it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you're pretty, you really enjoy what you do here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I do. As long as, it's usually when the hunters are here. Lots of times I don't get to bed until one o'clock in the morning and then I have to get up early to get them off hunting the next day. And if they're nice and they act like they appreciate it, I'm usually alright. But some of them are so hard to please that you just feel like you don't care.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You just look at that as a part of your work because this is your husband's work.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right, that's the only way that I can help him. And I do it mostly to save money. We could take him to a cafe to eat or to board him in a motel, but we wouldn't make much by the time we paid expenses.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is it hard to plan how to cook for all those men? Do you have trouble with it or are you pretty used to it now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, really I'm used to it because I even have to fix pretty good sized meals for just my family. But the hard part of it is not knowing what time they're going to be in to eat. And I like to fix something like spaghetti or stew or something that I can warm over when they're late. The last ones we had, there was three different groups and they didn't even all get here at the same time. So I'd feed part of them and then maybe a couple more would get here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was there ever much, a lot of cooking on the farm when you were a young girl?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just during haying season, my uncle and cousins used to come over and help put in the hay because my dad didn't own a hay baler. And when they were there, then there was extras to cook for. And my mother always cooked big meals just like most farms do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What would she cook? What kinds of foods would she cook?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When she had extras, she usually fixed a big roast and of course mashed potatoes and gravy. And she always baked pie or cake for company, which we didn't have too much for just us. She wasn't one to fix a lot of sweet desserts. So it was usually quite exciting for little kids around haying time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever have to help out in the kitchen during those times?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh yes, we always had to help. We peeled vegetables and of course we always had to help with dishes and things like that afterwards.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you girls have a lot of chores or did you feel you had a lot of time to play too?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I had quite a few chores because my sister was older and she didn't like to work outside. So usually I was the one that did the outside work. I always had to feed chickens and gather the eggs and I had to carry the wood for the wood cook stove, which we had until after I was married. And I had to milk the cows and separate the milk and help in the fields.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have a cream separator then or did you have to do it some other way?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, when I was smaller we had one that we turned and then later on he got an electric one and then I just plugged it in. But I always had to wash it afterwards and I hated that job.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You really hated it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I didn't like to wash the cream separator.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about feeding the chickens and all that, did you enjoy that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, just like most kids it kind of griped me because I was the one that always had to do it. But just getting at it was the worst part. It wasn't a hard job.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about carrying the wood, did you enjoy that or did you kind of begrudge it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I didn't mind that too much because it was in the basement and I didn't have to go outside in the cold to get it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did the wood stoves keep your house nice and warm?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh yeah, they had a real warm house. My dad was a real good carpenter and he had an old school house that he remodeled. And you'd never know it had ever been a school house now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How old was it, do you think, when it was built or anything like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, he got it before I was born, so I think it was quite old then. He put it on log skins and pulled it about five miles across the fields.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, so he moved it first?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, he had to move it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Wow, that's pretty interesting. A lot of hard work it sounds like.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, it took a good many years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And now down here in Kuski, do you belong to any community or church activities?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I am a member of Jehovah's Witnesses, but I don't belong to any community clubs of any kind.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there a reason for that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm just busy at home. I figure if I can take care of my family, that I've got enough work without belonging to any clubs.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You don't care too much for the social side of it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not really, no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about the children or Bob? Are they pretty much the same?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, Bob is worse than I am. He doesn't even like to go to a movie unless it's a drive-in. He just doesn't like to be around a lot of people.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you're a really close family unit, aren't you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think so, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It seems like to me when I watch everybody interact, it seems really close.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The boys have no desire to run around town evenings or anything like that. They're content to stay home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You haven't had any of your kids been into any of the same things a lot of kids today are?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, not that I know of. I've never had any trouble with them at all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The drug culture and all that, it just doesn't interest them at all?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. I'm sure they have never tried it. As far as I know, one beer is the most either one of them have ever drank at one time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Why do you think that your boys are so much... you don't have to worry about them the way a lot of parents would?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, their dad or I, neither one drink. And we have no desire to go out to dances or bars or anything like that. And they don't see us doing it. And I've tried to raise my kids by Bible principles. And they see us trying to live by what we teach them. And when I tell them something's wrong, I show them in the Bible where it says it's wrong and not just my idea.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you try to be an example to them?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you try to back it up with Bible teachings?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You can't tell a child not to do something and then they turn around and see you doing it. And expect them to have any faith in what you say.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And do they seem pretty respectful of the things that you teach them and things that you ask them to do and your ideas?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I think so.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That must make you feel good.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It does. I'm very proud of my boys and I've had a lot of compliments on them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are there any magazines or newspapers that your family subscribes to?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We take a few magazines, yes. Bob gets the hunting and fishing magazines. And I get a couple women's magazines.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Which ones would those be?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think it's Red Book and McCall's. I've just started getting them. And then we have the Bible study aids that we also read.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you enjoy your magazines pretty much?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What is it in them that you really enjoy?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I like the recipes and the patterns. And I like to read the short stories in them. And I just enjoy looking at the model homes and things like that. I like to sit and think of what I would like to do with my house if I could afford it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you have done most of your house yourself, haven't you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. Our house burnt down when we had been married five years. And we had no insurance and we already had three children. So we just started from scratch and built our own. And of course Bob was working a lot of the time and didn't have time to work on it. And so I just started doing what I could do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Of course, Bob's working doesn't get any kind of security or any kind of insurance?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, he usually logs enough to where he can draw a little unemployment in the winter time. And of course he pays in his social security. So if anything did happen to him, I might be able to draw social security for the children until they were 18.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you don't get any kind of medical insurance?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we have no medical insurance at all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is it pretty hard to make those bills if anything were to happen?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, yes. We have had quite a few doctor bills just this winter. But so far we've managed to get by. We are thinking of getting hospital insurance.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Wow. Hospital costs right now are...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, they're terrible.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you watch television?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Some. I would rather crochet in the evenings or write letters. There's certain programs that I watch.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What kind of programs do you enjoy?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, let's see. I like the animal shows. Animal World is real good. And I like the music shows. Mac Davis and the Irish Rover. I always watch them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What's that all about?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They're music.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They play music?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh. And then there's one that we like to watch. It's called Moving On. It's about a couple truck drivers. And I like it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. I bet Bob can kind of enjoy that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. He likes it as well as I do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about the news? Do you watch the news much?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, a little. I don't enjoy the news because it's such a wicked world that we're living in. It can really make a person depressed. And I listen enough to know what's going on, but that's about all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. Thinking back on your day-to-day life, what are the most common things that Bob would ask you about each day, or say when he'd come back in from the woods or something?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, he usually walks in and says, well, how did it go today? And just, it's mainly routine.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does he take pretty big interest in the children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. He's taken them with him. He started taking them steelhead fishing when they were about three or four years old. And he's taught them to shoot a gun when they were quite young. He's never allowed them to have a BB gun. He said they're going to shoot the real thing, and they're going to know what it can do. And he's nearly always got one of them with him when he's out hunting or checking traps or anything. He enjoys taking the boys and teaching them what he can.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about the girls? Do they get in on any of that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Becky gets to go once in a while if he isn't going to do a lot of walking. But, of course, she can't go and keep up with him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But it's okay for her to learn some of those outdoor things, too.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. He's taken her up and he's showed her a bear and a den. And he's showed her the deer and the elk and everything that he can.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, city kids would have to go to a zoo to see any of that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And, like I said, the kids know what mushrooms to pick. And we go berry picking all summer when there's berries to get. They love it. They've all learned fish. Shelly has even caught a fish.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And Shelly is pretty young, isn't she?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, she's three.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Wow. What about you? Your own life, does he ask you many things about how your day went or what's on your mind or anything like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: If he isn't too tired, sometimes he comes in at night and he'll sit down and fall asleep before I even have dinner ready. But we talk a lot, I think really more than most people. We talk about things that's happened. He leaves most of the business up to me to take care of. I even book most of the hunters for him. He usually gives me his check and he'll say, Now I want so-and-so amount for some certain thing and then I take the rest and pay bills and buy what has to be bought. He don't enjoy shopping at all. He don't even like to go into a grocery store if he can get out of it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But it sounds like you work pretty close together.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We do, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You just know what needs to be done and you just kind of...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He's right. And I usually leave most of the big decisions up to him. But half of the time he'll say, You do whatever you think. But if it's real important, we talk it over.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you ever get to do anything like travel or take any trips together?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Bob and I have taken one trip together and that was 17 years ago to go any distance. We go to Coeur d'Alene to visit my folks. But usually I stay home with part of the kids and the only trips he takes has to do with hunting. He's had to go to Boise and pick up a hunter because the plane was grounded or something like that. And he flies back in the mountains two or three times every winter to hunt.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you ever get to go on a plane trip with him?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. There's usually not room or I can't get away for that long with the kids in school. I have to pretty much stay here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You said before that you did get to go elk hunting. When was that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, about 10 years ago. I used to go elk hunting quite a bit, you know, just for the day. We'd come home at night. But I really enjoyed it. I went for several years. Since I've had the girls, I've kind of given that up.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever shoot an elk yourself?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: One.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have to pack it out yourself?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. I got it across the river and there was about five men that was following us in their car. And there was only one gun left that had any shells in it. And I spotted the elk and they didn't think I could hit it anyway, so they let me shoot at it. And when I killed it, well, then we had to all go across the river in the boat and we walked up to it. And one of the guys pulled the teeth out and handed them to me and then he handed me the hunting knife. And I just turned around and said, I'll see you at the river. So they dressed it out and then they packed it out later.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That must have been a pretty big thrill for you.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was. I was real proud of myself.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does Bob always hunt for all of the meat that you use here at Homewell's?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. This is the first year that we've ever had any beef. And he traded a bear hunt for a beef. But other than that, we have, oh, we've bought pork a couple times, but mainly we live on the deer and elk.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Deer and elk. And do you ever eat any bear meat or anything like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, Bob won't eat bear. The boys like it. They'll whack off some steaks off of a bear and cougar. They've eaten cougar.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Cougar meat, too. My gosh, I never heard of eating cougar.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It isn't too bad. If you didn't know what it was, you'd think it was pork. But just the thoughts of it, Bob won't eat it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have your own freezer or do you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. And I cut the meat myself.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You do? You cut all the different steaks and roasts and everything?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When I cut meat, there's steaks and roasts and hamburger and a little stew meat.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did you learn how to cut the meat?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: By trial and error.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Nobody sat you down and said, no, this is...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. If the grain all goes the same way, I cut steaks. And if it's too mixed up, well, we either put it in the hamburger or make a roast out of it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do you make hamburger?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I cut it up in little pieces and clean it up good, and then we take it down and have the meat market grind it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you have it ground for you? Yes. Do you use the liver and the other parts of the animal?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Bob won't eat heart or liver either, but we always give them to his folks. They like it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then you do the... clean the hides. Somebody... Bob cleans the hides.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we used to just throw them away, but this year we saved them for the fur buyer.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then he buys them and they have them tanned and other people can use the furs. That's pretty interesting. Does Bob set the carcass up for you so you can cut the meat, or do you have to do all that yourself?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I usually... he cuts it into quarters, which is really too big for me to handle, but I always manage it. And he brings them in in the morning before he leaves. And it takes me just 12 hours of steady cutting to cut a big elk, to cut and wrap it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So it's a whole day's project.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It is. It's all day and it's a mess.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do the girls watch you? I mean, have you ever tried to teach them anything?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't want them using the knives at all. And I bone it all out. I don't leave any bones in it at all. And of course we can use them for dog food.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah. You have quite a few hunting dogs and everything.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We have anywhere from 8 to 12, 14 dogs.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: To feed all the time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, we got it narrowed down now to about 8.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Wow. What about, do you sharpen your own knives and everything?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm not very good at it. I usually... The last fall we cut meat in the evenings and I got Bob to help me. But before that I'd just gather up all the knives I could find and he'd sharpen them before he left. And I'd just get by the best way I could.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you ever have a night, you know, you talk about all this work, do you ever have a night when you just say, oh heck, and open up a TV dinner or two? No. You never do?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't think that I have ever eaten a TV dinner.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You never order things out, you know, say from a pizza place or something?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There's no place around here to... Nothing?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No. So even after a day of butchering the meat, that you would sit down and you'd cook a big meal?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, usually something like that. I'll either cook a big pot of chili during the day or maybe I'll go buy some wieners and have hot dogs or something. Yeah. Or soup.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That sounds like a big job. What were some of the most important things to you when you decided to live in a small town, when you decided to live down here in Kuski or was it just expected that you would come down here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was expected. I had no choice. This was Bob's home and ever since the first time I had been down here, I loved this country. And I don't think I would ever want to go back to a farm. I like the mountains. Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And are there any relatives, immediate relatives living down here near you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: His mother and dad live very close to us, but they're the only relatives.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What kind of people are your neighbors?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, there's only one neighbor that we really know, and that's an old Indian man. And his daughter and her family have come back and moved in with him. And she's got little children that play with my two little girls, and they are one of the nicest families that you could ever live by.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And have you learned much from him or vice versa? Do you do much together?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Some. He will show you when to plant your garden and when to pick it. He's very good at gardening. Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And do the Indian people and the white people here in Kuski, do they get along pretty well?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Some of them. There's a lot of white people that are real fanatics about the Indians. But from what we have found, that there isn't really a lot of them that I would want to live by. They do have a habit of drinking. But the family by us, he doesn't drink at all. And I just can't think of a nicer person. Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's really interesting. How do the kids enjoy talking with Charlie?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. My girls have really liked him all their lives. In fact, when he came over and my youngest daughter was just real little, he picked her up, and she just grinned real big at him. And he told me, he said, this is the first baby, white baby I've ever held that wasn't scared of me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, wow.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And he just took to her, and he just loves her, and she thinks the world of him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But it took quite a while for Charlie to trust you, didn't it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was a long time. We've lived by now for over 14 years, and it's just been the last five years that I have really felt that he really liked us. Mm-hmm. They're hard to get acquainted with.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You have a picture here of yourself and your mother dressed in some Indian clothes and holding up an Indian rug. Can you tell me a little bit about that, or who it belongs to and how it was made, what it's made of?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Those are Charlie's clothes. He has two suitcases full of Indian clothes. And he offered to let my mother try on that dress. He said that I was too tall. And the dress weighs 40 pounds. The top part is solid beads, and the long white beads are made out of the backbone of steelhead, and they're worth 50 cents a piece.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, wow.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And they're only about a half an inch long, each bead. And those clothes are real valuable. He wouldn't sell them for any price.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Can he save these from when he was a young boy or something?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, his grandfather was an Indian chief. He's even got the chief's bonnet that he wore. But now some of his clothes aren't Nez Perce clothes. He said that some of them were from Montana.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So Charlie was a Nez Perce Indian?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about this rug? Do you know anything about that or whatever it is?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I'm not sure just exactly what it is. It isn't really a rug. I think that it was something the men tied around their waist and wore as kind of a skirt in front. And this is a handbag that my mother is holding.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What is that emblem supposed to mean? It looks like a hawk or an eagle?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's a bald eagle. The Indians used the eagle feathers for all of their headdress, and I think they've got some tradition about eagles.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And this is the American flag behind the eagle?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It looks like it. Yeah, it is.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And all of the silver work was handcrafted and everything, I suppose?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, it was all made by the Indians.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Wow, that's pretty interesting. Is there anything else that you can think of that you would like to tell me about your experiences as a rural woman?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, just that it takes a lot of hard work, and there's always something to be done. You never get it all done.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's kind of unique, you know, there aren't too many women that are married to a professional hunter and trapper, kind of a dangerous business. Are there any instances you can recall when you were really worried or had any big scares or things you had to contend with?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I used to worry an awful lot, but anymore, I guess you kind of get used to it, although I know if I stopped to really think about it that I could get upset. There's so many times when it takes a lot of bull hunters, and they will wound a bear, and then he has to take the dogs and go in and run it down, and sometimes they won't go up a tree, they just stop and fight the dogs. We've had dogs hurt awfully bad by a bear, and he's had a cougar jump out of the tree at him, and he would shoot it on the way down, and things like that. You never know how an animal is going to act.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you just kind of accept what your husband does?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I couldn't change his way of living if I tried, and I know that he would never be happy anywhere else, so I just do everything I can to help him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Has he ever tried to change your ways at all?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I changed my way of life quite a bit when I married him, because when I was in school, I liked to go to the school dances and dress up, and I liked to go to the...
